doc.title: Orrin Keepnews interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

chapter: Monk, the Army and learning the job
title: Committing to an artist rather than judging performances
summary: Once he signs an artist he trusts the artist's judgement, in keeping with being a catalytic agent.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: and signing artists, I approved of somebody, I liked what he was doing, I felt it made sense to me, should make sense to the world, I was willing to get involvement there, then I’m making a commitment at that point. That commitment involves working with that artist, getting from him as well as giving to him, but it does not necessarily involve my deciding that what he is doing at a given moment is good or bad, whether it meets with my approval is pretty God damned irrelevant. I am not more gifted than the artist in determining — this is a hard thing to articulate — I’m not talking about suspension of judgement. What I’m saying is I tend to make my judgements initially. I may revise them later but let’s let that go for the moment. If I have felt strongly enough positively about an artist to want to become involved in working with him that involves approving his taste. It has to involve approving his judgement. Therefore it involves that I am not going to nickel and dime the situation and decide that on this particular point I really know better than he does. And that’s where I part company with the people who feel that the only way they’re going to make their living is by making immediate sweeping judgements.
Isn’t part of your role in that situation to know not necessarily what is best, it’s what that performer is best — what his best is?

Yeah. Well again, when I speak of myself as a catalytic agent it’s endeavoring to provide the circumstances under which the artist can deliver to the best of his ability, not distracted or sidetracked or disturbed. And that implies of course — not necessarily my approval of what he is doing, it implies my approval of the rightness of his doing what he chooses to do.
